note: Teaching text, clarifying questions, inferred constraints and own examples. Inferred, not official. Examples are small generated inputs with outputs from the independent references in oracles.py.

clarifyingQuestions: May words contain characters missing from customOrder?
Is the input sorted in place or returned as a new list?
Can words be empty strings?
hints: Plain lexicographic order with a permuted alphabet is still lexicographic order.
Translate each word once into a key over the ordinary alphabet whose order matches customOrder.
Sort by translated keys with the library sort; the prefix rule then comes for free.
invariants: translation preserves the custom order: key(x) < key(y) exactly when x precedes y
a proper prefix always sorts first
chooseWhen: Many comparisons under a fixed non-standard alphabet
tradeoffs: Precomputed keys cost O(L) extra memory but make every comparison a native string comparison
hack2hire:67ce7ab08f73eb6319edd207.variantLabel: Inferred single variant: sort words under a custom alphabet

clarifyingQuestions: Do timestamps of writes arrive in increasing order?
What does get return when no version is old enough?
Does remove erase the past, or only hide the key from that time on?
What happens to a second write at the same timestamp?
hints: Because write times only grow, each key's versions are already sorted when appended.
A query for time t needs the last version with time <= t: a binary search for the insertion point.
Equal timestamps replace the last version instead of appending; remove simply drops the key's arrays.
invariants: each key's time array is strictly increasing
get never sees a version newer than its timestamp
tradeoffs: Keeping every version costs memory proportional to all writes; a compaction policy would bound it
hack2hire:69d3f7fd79bf03c0074bce16.variantLabel: Inferred level 1: versioned get with whole-key removal

clarifyingQuestions: Do timestamps of writes arrive in increasing order?
What does get return when no version is old enough?
Does remove erase the past, or only hide the key from that time on?
What happens to a second write at the same timestamp?
hints: Treat a deletion as just another version whose value is "absent".
Reads before the deletion time still find the older value by binary search.
remove first answers get(key, timestamp), then appends (or replaces) the tombstone.
invariants: each key's time array is strictly increasing
a tombstone hides the key only from its own time until the next set
chooseWhen: Audit-style stores where deletes must not rewrite history
tradeoffs: Tombstones are never compacted, so deleted keys keep their memory
hack2hire:69dd59d595e80ae213e5b7fc.variantLabel: Inferred level 2: deletions are versions too (time travel keeps old values)

clarifyingQuestions: Which entry is evicted among several with the same lowest rank?
Does get refresh an entry or change its rank?
Does updating an existing key ever evict?
Must the cache be thread-safe, and how would that be tested?
hints: Eviction needs the minimum of (rank, age) over the live entries: a priority queue.
Updating a key would require decrease-key; push a fresh heap entry instead and mark the old one stale.
When popping, skip entries whose write sequence differs from the map's current one.
invariants: the map holds at most capacity keys
every live key has exactly one non-stale heap entry
tradeoffs: Lazy deletion lets the heap grow with the number of writes, not the capacity

constraints: source has at most 1e5 rows with unique keys
clarifyingQuestions: Which entry is evicted among several with the same lowest rank?
Does get refresh an entry or change its rank?
Does updating an existing key ever evict?
Must the cache be thread-safe, and how would that be tested?
hints: A miss that the source can answer becomes a write into the cache.
Write-through keeps the source in sync, so evicted entries can be reloaded later with their latest value and rank.
Reuse the level-1 lazy heap for eviction and count loads separately.
invariants: the cache is always a subset of the source
getLoadCount equals the number of misses answered by the source
chooseWhen: Caches in front of slow stores
tradeoffs: Write-through doubles the work of each put but never loses updates on eviction
hack2hire:68aba144fc2e86fe2162e8a1.variantLabel: Inferred level 2: read-through, write-through ranked cache with a load counter

clarifyingQuestions: What does get return for a missing key?
Are transactions nested, and does commit close all of them?
What do rollback and commit return without an open transaction?
Must count be fast inside transactions?
hints: A hash map gives O(1) set, get and unset.
Use a sentinel ("") for missing keys since values are non-empty.
Removing an absent key must not fail.
invariants: the map holds exactly the keys set and not unset since
tradeoffs: None at this level

constraints: transactions may nest up to the call count
clarifyingQuestions: What does get return for a missing key?
Are transactions nested, and does commit close all of them?
What do rollback and commit return without an open transaction?
Must count be fast inside transactions?
hints: Copying the whole map at begin is simple but O(keys) per begin.
Instead record, per transaction, the old value of each key the first time it changes.
Rollback restores those old values; commit just drops all logs.
invariants: applying the innermost log restores the state at its begin
commit leaves the data unchanged
tradeoffs: An undo log makes rollback cost proportional to changes rather than to store size

clarifyingQuestions: What does get return for a missing key?

hints: Maintain a value-to-count map alongside the data.
Route every write (including undo during rollback) through one assign helper so counts stay right.
The undo log stays as in level 2.
invariants: count(v) always equals the number of keys holding v
rollback restores counts with the data
tradeoffs: A single write helper keeps every invariant in one place at a small call overhead
hack2hire:6920d4a994b324049c3251c1.variantLabel: Inferred level 3: transactions plus value counts
